claim: In Respect for Acting (1973) Hagen lists nine questions an actor must answer before acting even two minutes of ordinary life: who am I, what time is it, where am I, what surrounds me, what are the given circumstances, what is my relationship, what do I want, what's in my way, what do I do to get what I want. The six-step form often quoted (who am I, circumstances, relationships, want, obstacle, action) is the later condensation, usually attributed to A Challenge for the Actor (1991); it is not the list printed in Respect for Acting.
quote: Who am I? Character. What time is it? Century, year, season, day, minute. Where am I? Country, city, neighborhood, house, room, area of room. What surrounds me? Animate and inanimate objects. What are the given circumstances? Past, present, future, and the events. What is my relationship? Relation to total events, other characters, and to things. What do I want? Character, main and immediate objectives. What's in my way? Obstacles. What do I do to get what I want? The action: physical, verbal. ... These are the questions we must ask ourselves, and explore and define in order to act.
source: Hagen, U., with Frankel, H. (1973). Respect for Acting. New York: Macmillan. Reprinted without alteration, Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2008 (ISBN 978-0-470-22848-7), Part Two, 'The Object Exercises', Introduction, pp. 82-83. Text read from an online copy of the 2008 reprint, accessed 2026-10-12. Six-step version: Hagen, U. (1991). A Challenge for the Actor. New York: Scribner (not read; attribution from secondary summaries, e.g. Backstage, 'The Definitive Guide to Uta Hagen's Acting Technique').
establishes: A canonical American acting text holds that an actor settles identity, time, place, surroundings, prior and expected events, relationships, a main and an immediate objective, an obstacle, and actions before playing. Hagen gives the questions in order but says later in the same part that the order of examination matters less than covering them all.
doesNotEstablish: It does not measure whether answering the questions improves performance, how long it takes, or that any one question matters more than another. It is a teacher's prescription, not an observed regularity. It does not show that actors outside Hagen's tradition work this way.
population: Hagen's own students and practice (HB Studio, New York); the book is a teaching text for stage actors.
uncertainty: Wording verified verbatim against the reprint (pp. 82-83). The 1991 six-step attribution was not checked against A Challenge for the Actor itself. The task brief's six-question list matches the 1991 form, not the 1973 book.
designImplication: The source supports a scene brief carrying slots an actor fills before playing: who, when, where, surroundings, prior events, relationship, want, obstacle, and actions. Which slots SLATE shows, whether a student can play with some empty, and what an empty slot costs are SLATE's own choices; the source gives no weights and no cost.

claim: Stanislavski (Hapgood translation, 1936) has the teacher divide a play into large 'units' and then smaller ones, warns that the division is temporary and should use as few, large units as possible, and says that a creative objective lies at the heart of every unit. The objective must be named with a verb ('I wish to ...'), not a noun, because a noun leads the actor to illustrate a state rather than act.
quote: 'Imagine that this is not a turkey but a five-act play, The Inspector General. Can you do away with it in a mouthful? No; you cannot make a single mouthful either of a whole turkey or a five-act play. Therefore you must carve it, first, into large pieces ...' ... 'At the heart of every unit lies a creative objective.' ... 'you should not try to express the meaning of your objectives in terms of a noun. That can be used for a unit but the objective must always be a verb.' (OCR spacing corrected.)
source: Stanislavski, C. (1936). An Actor Prepares (E. R. Hapgood, Trans.). New York: Theatre Arts Books (Routledge reprint), Chapter 7, 'Units and Objectives', pp. 111-126 (quotes at pp. 111, 116, 123). Read from a scanned chapter excerpt, accessed 2026-10-12.
establishes: The founding Western acting text treats scene preparation as: divide the material into units, find the objective in each, phrase it as an active verb, and keep the units few and large so they mark a 'channel' through the play. It also says the divisions are for preparation only and fuse in performance.
doesNotEstablish: No measurement. It does not say how many units a scene has, how long division takes, or that dividing finer helps; it explicitly warns against dividing more than necessary. Hapgood's 'units/objectives' are translation choices (see the Benedetti entry).
population: A fictionalized acting class (Tortsov's students) written as a teaching novel; the prescriptions are Stanislavski's, drawn from Moscow Art Theatre practice.
uncertainty: Verbatim from a scanned copy of the Hapgood text (OCR errors such as 'ofevery' silently corrected). Page numbers from the scan's running heads.
designImplication: The source supports a brief that is broken into a small number of parts, each with one active objective, rather than a long list of details. The number of parts per scene and any reward for naming an objective as a verb are SLATE's own choices.

claim: Benedetti's 2008 translation renders the same chapter as 'Bits and Tasks' and defines Given Circumstances as everything given to the actor: plot, facts, incidents, period, time and place, way of life, the production's reading of the play, staging, design and sound. It also names the obstacle as a 'counter-Throughaction': every action meets a counter-action, and without that clash the play would have nothing for the characters to do.
quote: 'They mean the plot, the facts, the incidents, the period, the time and place of the action, the way of life, how we as actors and directors understand the play, the contributions we ourselves make, the mise-en-scène, the sets and costumes, the props, the stage dressing, the sound effects etc., etc., everything which is a given for the actors as they rehearse.' ... 'Every action meets a counter-action and the second evokes and strengthens the first. So, in every play, parallel to the Throughaction, there is an opposing counter-Throughaction coming from the opposite direction to meet it.'
source: Stanislavski, K. (2008). An Actor's Work: A Student's Diary (J. Benedetti, Trans. and Ed.). London and New York: Routledge. Given Circumstances: chapter on action, 'if' and given circumstances, pp. 52-53; counter-Throughaction: chapter on the Supertask and Throughaction, p. 318; chapter 7 is titled 'Bits and Tasks'. Read from an online copy, accessed 2026-10-12.
establishes: The given circumstances include the production's own interpretation and staging, not only the script's facts. The obstacle (counter-action) is treated as necessary to action rather than as an inconvenience. 'Bits and Tasks' is the closer rendering of Stanislavski's terms.
doesNotEstablish: It does not quantify anything, and does not say how to weigh a director's reading against the script's facts when they conflict.
population: As for An Actor Prepares: a teaching novel based on Moscow Art Theatre practice.
uncertainty: Verbatim from an online copy of the 2008 edition (the copy's provenance is unclear, so the publisher's page is given as the URL). Page numbers from that copy's running heads.
designImplication: The source supports treating a director's or casting note as part of the given circumstances (see topic 4) and treating the obstacle as part of the scene rather than an optional extra. Whether a brief always names an obstacle is SLATE's own choice.

claim: Hagen makes the obstacle a separate, required step and asks for it at three levels (character, main, immediate), including 'in the beats of the scenes'. She says that without an obstacle there is no drama, in tragedy and comedy alike.
quote: If I know what I want and can achieve my wishes readily without any problem, there is no drama. In tragedy and comedy and satire and farce--in anything that is worthy of the stage--conflict is at the root. Consequently, finding the obstacles to my objectives becomes imperative. ... Pose these questions against your character objectives, against your main objectives, and against your immediate objectives in the beats of the scenes.
source: Hagen, U., with Frankel, H. (1973). Respect for Acting. New York: Macmillan; Wiley reprint 2008, Part Three, 'The Obstacle', p. 180. Accessed 2026-10-12.
establishes: In this tradition the obstacle is a core element of scene analysis across genres, and objectives and obstacles nest (overall, main, immediate).
doesNotEstablish: It does not show that identifying the obstacle changes measurable performance quality.
uncertainty: Verbatim from the reprint.
designImplication: The source supports a brief that pairs each want with something in its way, at scene level and possibly per beat. The depth of nesting SLATE models is its own choice.

claim: Hagen defines a beat by its objective: it begins when an immediate objective sets in under given circumstances and ends when that objective succeeds or fails and new circumstances set in. She reports, unverified, that 'beats' came from Stanislavski's 'bits' said in a Russian accent. She also gives a turn inside one role: in A Month in the Country, Natalia's subconscious objective breaks into her awareness and her objective changes.
quote: A beat begins under a given set of circumstances when an immediate objective sets in. It ends when that objective has succeeded or failed and new circumstances set in. ... There is a point, later in the play, when Natalia's subconscious objective breaks through into her conscious awareness, and her objective becomes to punish herself for her baseness.
source: Hagen, U., with Frankel, H. (1973). Respect for Acting. New York: Macmillan; Wiley reprint 2008, Part Three, 'The Objective', p. 176. Accessed 2026-10-12.
establishes: A turning point within a scene is, in this tradition, the moment an objective is won or lost or the circumstances change, and a new immediate objective begins. A character can carry a conscious and a subconscious objective at once, and the turn can be one becoming the other.
doesNotEstablish: It does not say how many beats a scene has or how long a beat lasts. The etymology of 'beat' is explicitly hearsay.
uncertainty: Verbatim from the reprint.
designImplication: The source supports marking a scene's turning points as changes of objective or of circumstance, not as changes of mood alone. How many turns a brief contains, and how a student is judged on playing one, are SLATE's own choices.

claim: In Benedetti's translation, Tortsov corrects a student who says one line (happiness) stops and another (jealousy) begins in the Othello-Iago scene: the line does not stop, it is gradually changed by changing given circumstances, through bewilderment and doubt, and the earlier mood can even return. Small tasks are absorbed into larger ones.
quote: 'That, at this point, one line in the role, happiness, stops and a new line, jealousy, begins.' 'It hasn't stopped,' Tortsov corrected me, 'but is gradually taking on a new life because of changing Given Circumstances. First, it went through the brief period of happiness enjoyed by the newly married Othello, his joking with Iago, then bewilderment, bafflement, doubt, repulsion in the face of approaching unhappiness set in. Then jealousy abates, spontaneously, and the earlier mood of blissful happiness returns. We know these transitions from one mood to another in the real world.'
source: Stanislavski, K. (2008). An Actor's Work: A Student's Diary (J. Benedetti, Trans.). London: Routledge, chapter 'The Subconscious and the Actor's Creative State', p. 333. Accessed 2026-10-12.
establishes: Stanislavski describes a transition as graded and driven by circumstances, not as a switch from one feeling to the next, and allows an earlier state to return within the same stretch.
doesNotEstablish: It says nothing about the duration of a transition or how an observer would judge one. It is one worked example, not a general rule.
population: Teaching novel; Othello as the example.
uncertainty: Verbatim from an online copy of the 2008 edition.
designImplication: The source supports scoring a turn on whether it follows from what changed, rather than on how abrupt it is. Whether SLATE models a turn as graded or as a step, and any number on it, are SLATE's own choices.

claim: Shurtleff, a Broadway casting director, made 'Opposites' one of his twelve audition guideposts: whatever motivation the actor decides on, its opposite is also true and should be in the scene. This is the main practice source for holding two feelings at once rather than switching between them.
quote: No verbatim quotation verified against the book. Secondary summaries consistently give: 'Whatever you decide is your motivation in the scene, the opposite of that is also true and should be in it.' Acting Studio Chicago's summary: 'Whatever is true in the scene, the opposite is also true.'
source: Shurtleff, M. (1978). Audition: Everything an Actor Needs to Know to Get the Part. New York: Walker; Bantam paperback 1980. Guidepost 5, 'Opposites'. The book was not readable online (Internet Archive lending copy restricted); wording from secondary summaries: Acting Studio Chicago, 'Shurtleff's Guideposts' (undated), and search-result summaries. Accessed 2026-10-12.
establishes: A casting director's audition manual tells actors to play a want and its opposite together. Only secondary summaries were available, so only the gist is established.
doesNotEstablish: It does not establish that casting directors reward this, or that holding two feelings beats changing between them. A similar line attributed to Stanislavski ('When you play a good man, look for where he is evil') was found only in quotation sites and was not traced to a page of My Life in Art.
population: Shurtleff's audition classes and casting experience (Broadway and film).
uncertainty: Low for exact wording; moderate that the principle is as summarized, since the summaries agree.
designImplication: The source supports a brief that can ask for two contrary pulls at once (a 'mixture') as distinct from a turn from one to the other. Whether SLATE treats a mixture as harder than a turn, and by how much, is SLATE's own choice.

claim: Chekhov wrote to Mariya Lilina in 1903 that The Cherry Orchard had turned out 'not a drama, but a comedy, in places even a farce'; Stanislavski replied that it was a tragedy. Borny argues that in Chekhov's later plays the tragic and comic sides of a character's behavior are perceived at the same time (Vanya entering with flowers), unlike Shakespearean tragicomedy, which tends to alternate serious and comic scenes.
quote: A month after Chekhov had written to the actress Mariya Petrovna Lilina informing her that his new play, The Cherry Orchard, 'has turned out not a drama, but a comedy, in places even a farce', her husband Stanislavski wrote to the playwright and informed him that the play 'is not a comedy, nor a farce as you have written, this is a tragedy, whatever escape towards a better life you open up in the last act'. ... Chekhov's tragi-comedy is synthetic because the tragic and comic dimensions of a character's behaviour are perceived at the same time. Vanya's entry with a bunch of flowers for Helen in Act III of Uncle Vanya is both tragic and comic. In a Shakespearean tragi-comedy, by contrast, there is a tendency to alternate serious and comic scenes.
source: Borny, G. (2006). Interpreting Chekhov. Canberra: ANU E Press, Chapter 7, 'The Cherry Orchard: Complete Synthesis of Vision and Form'. Quotes Chekhov's letter to M. P. Lilina (15 September 1903) and Stanislavski's reply (October 1903); the letters themselves were not read in a published edition. Accessed 2026-10-12.
establishes: The playwright and the first director disagreed about whether the same text was comedy or tragedy, and a scholarly reading holds that Chekhov's characters are comic and grievous at once rather than by turns.
doesNotEstablish: It does not say how an actor plays the mixture, and the 'perceived at the same time' claim is Borny's interpretation of audience experience, not a measurement.
population: Chekhov's plays and their Moscow Art Theatre premieres; literary-critical argument.
uncertainty: Borny's text verified verbatim. Letter wording is as translated in Borny; dates from standard accounts, not checked against a letters edition.
designImplication: The source supports a brief that mixes comedy and grief in one moment, and supports that such a brief has no single correct register. Any difficulty value for a mixed register is SLATE's own choice.

claim: Spotlight, the UK casting directory, advises: learn the lines; frame a mid-close shot (chest to top of head) unless told otherwise; keep the eyeline close to the camera so both sides of the face are seen; a reader should not be too loud; plain (grey) background, soft light from in front, camera at eye level, landscape, stay close to the microphone; film an ident (slate) only if instructed; no more than about three takes before pausing; send more than one take only if they differ.
quote: Learn your lines and rehearse. ... Your eye line should be close to the camera as they want to see both sides of your face. If you're using a reader, make sure they aren't too loud. Don't go too far from the camera (unless you have an external microphone). Frame in a mid-close shot unless requested otherwise (mid-close shot means seeing from your chest to the top of your head). Don't do too many takes - If you can't get it in three takes, take some time to pause and then try again. Don't send too many takes, unless requested. If you send more than one take, make sure they're sufficiently different.
source: Spotlight. 'How to Self-Tape'. Spotlight News and Advice, by Spotlight Admin (undated page). Accessed 2026-10-12.
establishes: What a major casting body tells actors is conventional: reader off camera, eyeline just beside the lens, mid-close framing, lines learned, ident on request, few and distinct takes.
doesNotEstablish: Practice convention only. Nothing is measured: not that these settings change casting outcomes, nor by how much. The 'three takes' figure is advice, not data.
uncertainty: Verbatim from the live page. The page is undated and may change.
designImplication: The source supports a self-tape having a reader beside the lens, mid-close framing, optional slate, and a small number of deliberately different takes. Any score effect of framing or eyeline, and any take limit, are SLATE's own choices; the source gives none.

claim: UK industry bodies (Casting Directors' Guild, CPMA, Equity, PMA) agreed 2021 self-tape best practice: give actors tone, style and period; keep it simple (no props or home sets); four-day turnaround for up to six pages, three days for three pages or less; no more than two roles, two scenes per role and two versions of each scene; a reader helps but is not required and actors should not pay for one.
quote: '... a sense of tone, style of piece, period etc is incredibly useful, or a more detailed creative vision - a couple of lines from the director or lead creative where possible should be passed on.' ... 'casting directors should aim for a four-day minimum turnaround, with a maximum of six pages to learn in this time. Minimum turnaround for three pages or less would be three days. No artist should be asked to learn more than six pages for a first self-tape and there must not be more than two different roles asked for in one self-tape and no more than two scenes for each role, with no more than two versions of each scene.' ... 'A reader (this can be virtual, via a pre-recorded app, or in person - and the reader does not need to be an actor) is often beneficial to a good self-tape but should not be an absolute requirement.'
source: Casting Directors' Guild, Co-operative Personal Management Association, Equity and Personal Managers' Association (2021). Self-tape and Zoom audition best-practice guidelines, as reproduced in Backstage UK, 'Casting Directors + Equity UK Announce Guidelines for Self-Tape Auditions', 12 August 2021 (updated 13 August 2021). The bodies' own document was not located; quotations are from the Backstage reproduction. Accessed 2026-10-12.
establishes: Agreed UK limits on the size of a self-tape request (pages, roles, scenes, versions) and the norm that casting supplies tone, style and period, plus a director's note where possible.
doesNotEstablish: Negotiated best practice, not law and not measurement; says nothing about how tapes are judged.
population: UK scripted drama casting (film, TV, theatre).
uncertainty: Quotations verified verbatim in the Backstage reproduction; secondary relative to the bodies' own text.
designImplication: The source supports a brief that carries tone, style and period plus an optional director's line, and caps a request at about two scenes and two versions each. Those caps are practice limits SLATE may adopt; any SLATE number beyond them is its own choice.

claim: Under the 2023 SAG-AFTRA TV/Theatrical agreement, sides must arrive at least 48 hours before a self-tape (72 for minors), a first self-tape is capped at 8 pages and a callback at 12, the actor cannot be required to memorize, and no stunts, nudity or specific software or equipment may be required. This conflicts with Spotlight's 'learn your lines': memorization is conventional in the UK guidance and contractually optional in the US.
quote: Sides shall be provided to actors at least 48 hour prior to self-tape (72 hours for minors); 8 pages maximum for first self-tape, 12 pages for call-backs; actor cannot be required to memorize sides. No stunts or nudity; no use of specific software or equipment.
source: SAGindie (SAG-AFTRA). 'NOTICE: Theatrical Contract Changes (2023)', by Will Prescott, 17 January 2024, summarizing the 2023 SAG-AFTRA TV/Theatrical Contracts. The union's own contract bulletin on self-tapes (June 2024) exists but could not be fetched. Accessed 2026-10-12.
establishes: US union terms for self-tape requests: preparation time, page caps, separate (larger) cap for callbacks, and that memorization cannot be required.
doesNotEstablish: Contract terms, not craft guidance; says nothing about eyeline, framing or what casting rewards.
population: SAG-AFTRA performers under the TV/Theatrical contracts.
uncertainty: Verbatim from the SAG-affiliated summary; the full contract text was not read.
designImplication: The source supports a callback being a larger, distinct request from a first tape, and supports memorization being a choice rather than a rule. Whether SLATE scores memorized versus held sides differently is SLATE's own choice.

claim: Caroline Liem, a Los Angeles casting director, advises placing the reader next to the camera, about one step away, at the actor's eye level, speaking more quietly than the actor because the reader is nearer the microphone; slate only if asked; memorize the sides before taping.
quote: Place your reader next to the camera, about one step away from it. Remember to direct your reader to speak at a lower volume than you as he or she is closer to the microphone than you are. Be mindful to have your reader at eye level with you as well. (Section headings also read: 'Slate (if asked)'; 'Memorize your sides before taping'.)
source: Liem, C. (2018, 8 November). 'A Casting Director's 12 Rules for the Perfect Self-Tape'. Backstage. Only part of the article body was accessible. Accessed 2026-10-12.
establishes: A working US casting director's version of the same conventions as Spotlight: reader beside the lens at eye level, quiet reader, slate on request, lines memorized.
doesNotEstablish: One practitioner's advice; no data.
uncertainty: The reader paragraph is verbatim; the other rules were seen only as headings.
designImplication: Corroborates the conventions in the Spotlight entry. Nothing here gives SLATE a number.

claim: After students propose many different verb-objectives for the same Brand scene, Stanislavski's teacher says each was in its way true and produced action, and that which one works depends on the actor: an objective must attract and excite that actor. More than one reading of a unit is valid.
quote: 'Every one of the objectives you have chosen is, in a way, true, and calls for some degree of action,' said the Director. 'Those of you who are of a lively temperament might find little to appeal to your emotions in "I wish to remember my dead child". You would prefer "I wish to take hold of him and never let go". ... Others would be unmoved by that. So it is important that an objective have the power to attract and to excite the actor.' (Hapgood; OCR spacing corrected.) Benedetti renders the first sentence: 'Each one of the Tasks you selected was true in itself and to one degree or another produced action.'
source: Stanislavski, C. (1936). An Actor Prepares (E. R. Hapgood, Trans.), Chapter 7, p. 126; and Stanislavski, K. (2008). An Actor's Work (J. Benedetti, Trans.), Chapter 7, 'Bits and Tasks', p. 151. Accessed 2026-10-12.
establishes: The founding text holds that one unit admits several true objectives, and that the right one is partly a property of the actor.
doesNotEstablish: It does not say how a director or casting director chooses among valid readings, or that all readings are equal; Stanislavski also lists objectives he calls wrong (mechanical, exhibitionist, too general).
uncertainty: Verified verbatim in both translations.
designImplication: The source supports scoring a reading on whether it is specific, active and played through, rather than against one correct answer. It also supports some readings being wrong (vague, showing off, aimed at the audience). How SLATE grades specificity is its own choice.

claim: Hagen shows that A Streetcar Named Desire has been produced under two opposite readings (Blanche as victim; Blanche as destroyer), with character relationships 'diametrically opposed'. She says the director has the final say on the reading and that a well-trained actor should be able to justify and execute almost any direction.
quote: Whether or not your definition is correct will finally be the director's decision or an agreement between the two of you. ... The play has also been produced as a plea for a down-to-earth, rational life ... Consequently, the relationships of the characters to the play and to each other become diametrically opposed. ... [the actor] should have at his fingertips a technique so flexible that he can justify almost any direction he is given, and execute it in terms of his personal realities.
source: Hagen, U., with Frankel, H. (1973). Respect for Acting. New York: Macmillan; Wiley reprint 2008, Part Three, 'First Contact with the Play', pp. 148-150. Accessed 2026-10-12.
establishes: One play supports opposite valid readings in production; the director's reading, once given, is what the actor executes; following a direction is a skill.
doesNotEstablish: It does not measure how often directors and actors disagree, or how auditions judge readings.
population: American professional theater practice as Hagen reports it.
uncertainty: Verbatim from the reprint.
designImplication: The source supports a brief with no single right reading, and a director's note, once given, becoming a requirement that the next attempt is judged against. How strictly SLATE enforces a note is its own choice.

claim: Joanna Merlin, casting director for Harold Prince's Broadway productions and for The Last Emperor, says the actor never knows what the director wants, so the actor should make strong choices; a director will stop an interesting actor with a different reading and ask for it another way, while a 'straight reading' reveals nothing. If the actor asks a question at the audition and the answer changes things, the actor is obligated to make that adjustment.
quote: The actor never knows what the director is looking for. You can't second-guess the director. And oftentimes, the director is not sure what he or she is looking for. However, if the actor seems interesting and is doing something that's totally different (and the actor is only going to seem interesting if he's made strong choices), then the director will stop him and ask him to do it another way. But if the actor goes in doing the so-called "straight reading," the straight intelligent reading, he is not going to reveal himself as an actor. ... the auditors may give you an answer that changes everything that you've worked on, and you are obligated to make that adjustment.
source: Eaker, S. (2001, 20 February). 'Audition Advice From an Industry Vet: Joanna Merlin'. Back Stage (interview drawn from Merlin, J. (2001). Auditioning: An Actor-Friendly Guide. New York: Vintage). The book itself was not read. Accessed 2026-10-12.
establishes: A casting director's statement that casting judges strong, committed choices rather than a correct reading, and that an adjustment, once given, binds the actor.
doesNotEstablish: One practitioner's view; no data on how often strong but different choices are cast.
population: US theater and film casting (Merlin's career).
uncertainty: Verbatim from the interview.
designImplication: The source supports rewarding commitment and specificity on an unadjusted first attempt, and judging a later attempt on whether it took the given adjustment. The relative weights are SLATE's own choice.

claim: Hagen on readings, including cold readings: give yourself an objective and go for it with real improvised actions, because a director will hold an actor for reality, not interpretation.
quote: What you should do at a reading, even a cold reading for which you have been given little or no time to prepare, is to go out on a limb: give yourself an objective and then head for it with improvised actions which are as real as possible. ... Even a mediocre director will hold you because of your reality, not on your interpretation.
source: Hagen, U., with Frankel, H. (1973). Respect for Acting. New York: Macmillan; Wiley reprint 2008, Part Three, 'Auditions', p. 204. Accessed 2026-10-12.
establishes: A teacher's claim that auditions reward a committed objective and believability over a particular interpretation.
doesNotEstablish: Not measured; Hagen's opinion.
population: Hagen's experience of New York auditions.
uncertainty: Verbatim.
designImplication: Agrees with Merlin. The source supports believability and commitment counting more than which valid reading was chosen; the weighting is SLATE's own choice.

claim: Hagen holds that style and genre labels (realistic, romantic, farcical, tragicomic, absurd and so on) are applied to a work after it exists, by observers, and that an actor cannot predetermine style; the form comes from the content. Three Odets plays explored for their content would yield three different 'styles'.
quote: Style is the dirtiest word in the actor's vocabulary. ... in the act of creation, whether it be a baby or a role in a play, you cannot predetermine style (shape, sound or form). ... Remember that all of the labels you are familiar with (realistic, surrealistic, romantic, satirical, farcical, tragicomic, naturalistic, classical, neo-classical, avant-garde, theater of the absurd, theater of cruelty, etc.) were stuck onto a piece of work after it came into existence and not before. ... If a director and a group of actors would have a full experience with the content of Awake and Sing, Rocket to the Moon, and The Country Girl, they would arrive at three different "styles" in their productions, although all three plays were written by Odets.
source: Hagen, U., with Frankel, H. (1973). Respect for Acting. New York: Macmillan; Wiley reprint 2008, Part Three, 'Style', pp. 217-219. Accessed 2026-10-12.
establishes: A major acting text argues that the material's content, not its genre label, decides what the actor does.
doesNotEstablish: It is an argument, not evidence; screen-acting and comedy specialists disagree in places (e.g. on timing technique). It does not show that genre has no effect.
uncertainty: Verbatim. One school's position.
designImplication: The source supports deriving a brief's demands from the scene's content (wants, obstacles, turns, register) rather than from a genre tag alone. Whether SLATE keeps a genre tag as a summary of those demands is its own choice.

claim: Hagen says what makes a fight tragic, ugly or funny is its cause, its objective and the relationship, not a comic manner, and gives A Phoenix Too Frequent: an actress who plays the widow's grief out of context may be truthful but not truthful to the play, which is a comedy about the desire for life.
quote: What makes a fight between two people tragic, ugly, or funny? It is the cause of the fight, the objective of the fight, and the relationship between the fighters. ... If comedic material gets heavy or unfunny, the director or the actor, or both of them, have left out something inherent in the material.
source: Hagen, U., with Frankel, H. (1973). Respect for Acting. New York: Macmillan; Wiley reprint 2008, Part Three, 'Style', pp. 219-220. Accessed 2026-10-12.
establishes: In this tradition, comic or tragic register follows from circumstances, objective and relationship within the material; misreading the material, not lacking a comedy technique, makes comedy fail.
doesNotEstablish: It does not deny that comedy has its own skills (timing, pace); it is silent on them. No measurement.
uncertainty: Verbatim.
designImplication: The source supports a brief's register coming from its circumstances and relationships. Any separate 'comedy skill' in SLATE would be SLATE's own choice and is not supported by this source.

claim: Casting practice does treat tone, style and period as information an actor needs: the UK guidelines ask casting to pass them on. A casting podcast frames horror, fantasy and period work as the problem of grounding a performance truthfully in a heightened world, which is a material-demands framing rather than a separate technique per genre.
quote: '... a sense of tone, style of piece, period etc is incredibly useful ...' (CDG/Equity guidelines, 2021). 'Want to know the key to grounding an acting performance in a heightened world? Emmy and Artios Award-winning Casting Director Suzanne Smith ... joins host Robert Peterpaul to explore the craft of acting truthfully in fantasy, horror, and period stories.' (episode description only.)
source: CDG, CPMA, Equity and PMA (2021) guidelines, as reproduced in Backstage UK, 12 August 2021; and Casting Networks, 'How to Act Truthfully in Horror & Fantasy Genres with Casting Director Suzanne Smith' (How We Role podcast), 30 October 2025 (only the episode description was read). Accessed 2026-10-12.
establishes: Casting bodies treat genre and tone as relevant briefing information. The podcast description shows a casting director framing genre work as truthfulness under heightened circumstances.
doesNotEstablish: Nothing about what specific technique horror, comedy or period work requires, and nothing measured. The podcast content itself was not reviewed. Backstage articles on horror auditions (2019) were not accessible beyond their headlines.
uncertainty: The guideline quote is verbatim; the podcast is a blurb only. Weak evidence for any genre-specific technique claim.
designImplication: The source supports a brief stating its genre and tone as information for the actor. It does not support genre labels carrying technique requirements; any genre-to-skill mapping in SLATE is SLATE's own choice and should be stated as such.

claim: Casting guidance treats a second take or version as a different choice, not a copy: Spotlight says multiple takes should be sufficiently different; the UK guidelines allow no more than two versions of a scene; the SAG-AFTRA agreement gives callbacks a separate, larger page cap.
quote: Don't send too many takes, unless requested. If you send more than one take, make sure they're sufficiently different. (Spotlight) ... no more than two scenes for each role, with no more than two versions of each scene. (CDG/Equity 2021) ... 8 pages maximum for first self-tape, 12 pages for call-backs. (SAGindie summary of the 2023 SAG-AFTRA agreement)
source: Spotlight, 'How to Self-Tape' (undated); CDG, CPMA, Equity and PMA guidelines (2021) as reproduced in Backstage UK; SAGindie, 'NOTICE: Theatrical Contract Changes (2023)' (2024). Accessed 2026-10-12.
establishes: Practice convention: a re-attempt for casting exists to show another choice or a requested version, and the number of versions is kept small.
doesNotEstablish: No evidence on whether a second version raises casting chances, or by how much.
uncertainty: All three verified verbatim; convention, not measurement.
designImplication: The source supports a retake being worth something only if it differs (a new choice or the requested adjustment), with few retakes allowed. A retake that only repeats the first should gain little; how little is SLATE's own choice.

claim: Merlin describes the adjustment as the reason for a second attempt in the room: the director stops an actor and asks for the scene another way, and directors schedule time to 'give them adjustments'. An actor who waits for the adjustment instead of making a choice is less wanted.
quote: ... you can't predict when the director will want to take more time to work with someone--give them adjustments and so on. But that actor can be you. ... then the director will stop him and ask him to do it another way. ... The director feels he can collaborate with the actor who makes strong choices. There's much more desire to work with that person than someone who comes in and waits for the director to give him an adjustment.
source: Eaker, S. (2001, 20 February). 'Audition Advice From an Industry Vet: Joanna Merlin'. Back Stage. Accessed 2026-10-12. The last sentence was in a search-result extract of the same interview; the page text was cut off just before it, so it is partly unverified.
establishes: In audition practice a re-attempt is usually driven by an adjustment from the director, and the adjustment is a test of collaboration (taking direction).
doesNotEstablish: No data on callback rates or on how adjustments are scored.
uncertainty: The first two sentences are verbatim; the last is from a search extract of the same interview.
designImplication: The source supports a second attempt being judged on whether it took the given note, and the first on whether it committed to a choice. Weights are SLATE's own choice.

claim: Stanislavski and Hagen both say a repetition must be re-created, not copied. When students repeat a search for a purse they had already found, the teacher sees no objectives, action or truth, because the reason for searching was gone. Hagen requires that an exercise be repeatable 'as if for the first time' and describes long runs as the challenge of living a role anew each night.
quote: We put the purse back where it had been and we began to hunt it. Only this time we did not have to search because the object had already been found once. As a result we accomplished nothing. 'No. I saw neither objectives, activity nor truth, in what you did,' was Tortsov's criticism. (Hapgood, OCR spacing corrected.) ... you should be able to repeat a precisely defined concept broken down into actable elements (comparable to the score of a musician), as if it were happening for the first time. (Hagen, p. 86)
source: Stanislavski, C. (1936). An Actor Prepares (E. R. Hapgood, Trans.), Chapter 8, 'Faith and a Sense of Truth', p. 127; Hagen, U., with Frankel, H. (1973). Respect for Acting, Wiley reprint 2008, pp. 86 and 206. Accessed 2026-10-12.
establishes: In these texts, repeating the same material is valuable only if the actor rebuilds the objective and circumstances; a mechanical repeat is worthless or worse.
doesNotEstablish: No measurement of how repetition affects quality, nor of fatigue or diminishing returns. Says nothing about casting.
uncertainty: Verbatim in both.
designImplication: The source supports repeated work on the same scene improving only when something is newly chosen or re-created, and a plain repeat adding little. The size of any gain or decay is SLATE's own choice.

claim: What was searched for and not found, or found only in secondary form.
quote: No verbatim quotation verified. Summary of searches: (1) No measured data on how long an actor's scene breakdown takes, or on whether breakdown improves rated performance; the acting texts are prescriptive. (2) No measurement of transfer of acting skill between genres (comedy to drama, horror reaction work), and no primary screen-acting text on genre technique was read; Backstage horror-audition articles (2019) and the Suzanne Smith podcast were accessible only as headlines or blurbs. (3) No empirical study of how casting directors judge self-tapes was found; the claim that casting decides in the first seconds appears only in commercial blogs with no data. One academic article was found but not read: Smith, K. (2025). 'Taping into the void': acting labour, self-tapes, and resistance in the digital economy. Studies in Theatre and Performance, 45(2), 124-137 (doi:10.1080/14682761.2025.2500130). It is a labor study, not a measure of judgment. (4) The Casting Society of America's own self-tape guidance was not found; SAG-AFTRA's pages and contract bulletin returned 403, so the 2023 terms come from the SAGindie summary. (5) Shurtleff's Audition (1978) and Michael Chekhov's To the Actor (1953) were not readable online (restricted lending copies); Shurtleff's 'Opposites' and Chekhov's claim that individual feeling can coexist with a contrasting atmosphere are from secondary summaries only. (6) The Stanislavski line 'when you play a good man, look for where he is evil' was found only on quotation sites. (7) No source gives a number of beats per scene, a beat length, or a callback rate.
source: Searches via web search and fetch, 2026-10-12; Internet Archive metadata for Shurtleff (auditioneverythi00shur) and M. Chekhov (toactorontechniq00chek) showed access-restricted items; Crossref metadata for doi:10.1080/14682761.2025.2500130.
establishes: The evidence for this area is acting-teacher prescription and casting-body convention. None of it is measurement.
doesNotEstablish: Absence of evidence here is not evidence that such data do not exist; only English-language, openly accessible sources were searched.
uncertainty: Search coverage was moderate; paywalled trade press (Backstage, Deadline) and union PDFs blocked several fetches.
designImplication: Every number in SLATE's self-tape briefs (beats per scene, preparation time, retake value, genre difficulty, framing penalties) will be SLATE's own choice. None should be presented as research-derived.
